feedback: Written before this candidate has raced; no outcome is claimed for it. Evidence: iteration 0 is the only stable design (oval 20/20 at 1.65 s, score 356.6). The integration needed no controller compensation for this geometry, because it is the same platform the controller was tuned against. Iteration 3 (y=0.07) and iteration 4 (y=0.03) show that sensor lead is a sharp optimum at y=0.05. Iterations 5 and 6 show that the 8 mm and 16 mm footprints also collapse the oval, so the 12 mm footprint is the reference. Iteration 7 shows the ±0.032 m spread collapses the oval with the baseline drivetrain, so the iteration-2 bend gain was not a real spread effect. Iteration 8 (body 0.12 m) is the last geometry change tested, and its outcome is not yet known to me. For the next design, I suggest holding the sensor row fixed and testing drivetrain settings one at a time. If the oval is still 20/20 near 1.65 s with the body at 0.12 m, keep the shorter body and test wheel_track alone. If the oval drops, return to body_length 0.16 m and test wheel_track alone. If the bends (s-bend 0.17, slalom 0.12) do not move under any geometry change while the oval stays at 20/20, the remaining limit is controller-side and the final geometry should stay at the baseline.
requested_changes: If the iteration-8 body-length change (0.12 m) collapsed the oval, keep body_length 0.16 m and change wheel_track alone from 0.12 to 0.11 m at 0.6 kg, since iteration 1 never isolated the track effect from the 0.5 kg mass.

If the oval holds at 20/20 near 1.65 s with lower oscillation, keep body_length at 0.12 m and test wheel_radius 0.032 m alone at 0.6 kg, to check whether a small speed gain helps the bends without disturbing the oval.
Keep sensor y at 0.05 m, sensor_size at 0.012 m and x at ±0.024 m, because iterations 3 to 7 show each of these collapses the oval when changed alone.
